prompt_context_by_prefix.lpn:
Use these preferred technical term translations when relevant:
- flow (Q): caudal
- velocity (v): velocidad
- head (H): carga
    DO NOT render as: a lazy anatomical calque that is NOT the language's natural hydraulic term — but an anatomically-derived word that IS the dominant local standard is correct (English 'head' is itself the body-part word repurposed); defer to the cultural standard, do not 'fix' a natural term for containing a body-part morpheme; pressure (head is a length/energy-per-weight, not a pressure); source/origin of a stream
- head loss (h_L): pérdida de carga
    DO NOT render as: pressure loss / pressure drop (use the head-loss term, not the pressure term); a lazy anatomical calque that is not the local standard — an anatomically-derived word that IS the dominant standard is correct; see 'head' root entry
- friction loss (h_f): pérdida por fricción
- minor loss (h_m): pérdida localizada
- pressure (p): Presión aguas arriba
    DO NOT render as: the HEAD term (a height of water column) — pressure here is what a gauge reads; atmospheric or meteorological pressure senses; a stress or material-strength sense; figurative 'pressure' (urgency, coercion)
- elevation (z): Elevación aguas arriba
    DO NOT render as: the HEAD term — an elevation is a position above a datum, not an energy; a generic 'tall/high' adjective where the language has a surveying term; altitude in the aviation or geographic sense where a levelled survey term exists
- demand: Demanda
    DO NOT render as: economic or market demand; a legal demand/claim; a request in the everyday sense
- static head (H): Carga estática de suministro
    DO NOT render as: electrostatic / static electricity; 'stationary/motionless' in a non-hydraulic sense
- maximum allowable head (H): Presión máx. adm. tubería
    DO NOT render as: the operating / computed head (this is a fixed design limit, not the pressure the network actually develops)
- supply head (H): Carga de suministro
    DO NOT render as: an economic 'supply'; confusing supply (source) head with the delivered/residual head at a demand point
- supply curve: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: an economic supply curve; a demand curve
- looped network: red de tuberías mallada
    DO NOT render as: a control-flow / programming loop; a physical loop, knot, or coil
- branched network: Red de tuberías ramificada
    DO NOT render as: a literal botanical 'tree' where the language has a proper network/graph term; a looped or meshed network (branched means no loops)
- pipe line: Tramos de tubería
    DO NOT render as: a queue or line of people; a rope, cord, or cable; a line of text; a purely geometric line/segment
- pressure rating: Presión máx. adm. tubería
    DO NOT render as: a stress or material strength rather than a water pressure; blood-pressure or tyre-pressure senses; a general word for strong or high
- pressure reduction: reducción de presión
    DO NOT render as: naming a specific device (break pressure tank, BPT, pressure-reducing valve) as if the tool recommends one; depressurizing in the sense of emptying or draining the pipe
- energy grade line (EGL): línea de energía
- Manning roughness (n): coeficiente de rugosidad de Manning
- friction factor (f): factor de fricción
- draw (a diagram): [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: draw water (abstract, pump, or take water from a source) -- the wrong sense here, and PLAUSIBLE in a hydraulics context, which is what makes it dangerous; pull, drag, or haul; draw as in a lottery or a tie/stalemate; withdraw money
- junction: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a road junction, crossroads, or intersection; a physical pipe fitting (tee, cross, elbow) -- a junction here is a point in the model, not a part you buy; a railway junction; an electrical junction box
- reservoir: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a tank whose level changes over time -- lpn_ explicitly does NOT model tanks (see lpn_notes_2_def), and calling this one would promise time-varying behaviour that does not exist; a natural lake specifically, where the language has a general storage/supply term; a reserve or reservation in the non-physical sense
- node: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a computing/server node (a transliterated loanword where the language has a real graph or network-diagram term); a knot, lump, or swelling (the anatomical/botanical sense of the Latin root); a node in the wave-physics sense (a point of zero amplitude)
- link: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a hyperlink or web link -- the dominant modern sense of the English word, and the wrong one here; a chain link (the physical object); a connection in the social or logistical sense
- vertex: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a mathematical vertex of a polygon or a parabola apex, where the language has a plainer word for a bend or corner point in a drawn line; a peak or summit; a vertex in the anatomical sense (crown of the head)
- background image: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a backdrop in the theatrical/stage sense (the English source word was CHANGED to "background image" in Task 193 precisely to remove this transliteration lure); a wallpaper or decorative background; an online/satellite map layer -- this is a plain image file the user already has
- pump curve: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a curve in the geometric/road sense; a pump characteristic confused with an efficiency or power curve -- this one is head against flow
- project (saved network): [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: an engineering project or job in the contractual sense (a scheme, a works, a contract) -- this is a saved document; a projection (optical or cartographic); to project or forecast
- scenario: [needs translation sprint]
    DO NOT render as: a scene or setting in the dramatic/film sense; a scenario in the "worst case story" narrative sense, where the language has a modelling or variant-case term; a copy or duplicate of the network -- a scenario is a set of differences, not a second network
- upstream: aguas arriba
- downstream: aguas abajo

lpn.context: Hydraulic head — energy per unit weight of water, expressed as a height of water column. The ROOT concept behind head loss, velocity head, weir head, and gross/net head. A length, never a pressure. Appears as a bare label in Weir Flow (ws_headWaterHeight), Orifice (or_head), and Manning Pipe Flow (mpf_velocity_head). Acceptable English synonyms (translate the concept, not the exact word): energy elevation, hydraulic grade line (HGL).
lpn.translation_notes: Newly seeded 2026-07-20 to close the long-standing gap where only the COMPOUNDS (head loss, velocity/weir/gross/net head) had entries but the root word 'head' did not — the root is what every agent re-derived (and sometimes mistranslated as anatomical head or pressure). Values below are the roots extracted from those compound entries and are best-effort/derived, not natively verified — confirm in the term-centric sweep (see ROADMAP). Several languages split the root by sense: the hydro-power 'fall' sense uses a different word than the pipe 'head' sense (cs spád vs tlaková výška; hr/sr visina·pad vs visina; ro sarcină vs cădere; tr yük vs düşü; ar علو/الارتفاع vs الضغط). Where that split exists, keep the pipe/energy-head root here and let the fall-sense compounds keep their own word. Slavic напор/напір, sw kimo (corrected from kichwa — see 2026-07-22 note below), and the هد/ہیډ/ہیڈ/हेड/ሄድ loanword family are consistent and documented across the suite (see 'head loss' notes). [2026-07-21 Task 128 RESOLVED — Tom decision] Native review is not realistically available for these; rely on AI guidance and defer to the locally natural term. lpn.context: Water pressure as a gauge would read it, in psi / kPa / bar / m or ft of water. Distinct from HEAD, which is the same energy expressed as a height of water column. Appears as the upstream input and downstream residual on the waterline calculators (Hazen-Williams hw_pressure_up/hw_pressure_down, Darcy-Weisbach) and in the negative-pressure check.
lpn.translation_notes: Created 2026-07-28 (ROADMAP Task 166 sprint) to close a real gap: the suite had entries for 'head', 'head loss' and 'pressure rating' but none for the bare concept, so every agent re-derived it and the head-vs-pressure trap had to be re-explained in each sprint prompt. Values below are the ATTESTED LABEL FORMS of hw_pressure_up ('Upstream pressure') as each language's own agent wrote it in this sprint, independently re-verified afterwards — read the pressure word out of the phrase, not the whole label. Every language landed on its ordinary water-pressure word and none reached for the head term. Note the pre-existing ar tension: head loss there is 'فقدان الضغط', which reads literally as 'pressure loss' while pressure itself is 'ضغط'; this is long-standing shipped ar usage and was deliberately not touched by this sprint (see ROADMAP if it is ever revisited).

lpn.context: Height of a point above a datum — ground, pipe invert, or water surface. On the waterline calculators the user enters the upstream and downstream elevations (hw_elev_up / hw_elev_down) and the page derives the HGL and the residual pressure from them.
lpn.translation_notes: Created 2026-07-28 (ROADMAP Task 166 sprint). Values are the ATTESTED LABEL FORMS of hw_elev_up ('Upstream elevation') as each language's own agent wrote it, independently re-verified. Most languages used their surveying term for a levelled height (kota / cotă / Cote / quota / отметка / тераз), not a generic 'height' word; where a file already had an established elevation word elsewhere (mi_elevation, or_centroid_elev) the agent matched it rather than inventing one. Do not conflate with HEAD: an elevation is measured from a datum, a head is an energy expressed as a height.

keys_to_translate.lpn_notes_2_def: Tanks, water quality, and control valves that open and close on their own (PRV, PSV, FCV) are not modeled. A pipe can carry a fixed minor loss, but not a valve whose open or closed state depends on the flow being solved for.

When a project file is kept on a shared drive, this page tells you if a colleague already has it open, so that two people do not write over each other. Because this is an early preview, please use it for small networks and for testing only.
keys_to_translate.lpn_notes_5_def: A pump follows H = H₀ − aQ^b, where H is the head the pump adds and Q is the flow through it. Enter one, two, or three points from the manufacturer's curve. Three points — the head at zero flow, the normal working point, and the point of highest flow — fit H₀, a and b directly, and follow a published curve most closely. Two points fit a parabola (b = 2) with its peak at zero flow. One point uses a common rule: the head at zero flow is 1.33 × the head you enter, and the highest flow is 2 × the flow you enter, which again gives b = 2. A pump with no points entered adds no head at all. The curve is not stopped at zero, so asking a pump for more flow than its curve can deliver gives a negative head. The fix is a bigger pump or a smaller demand, not a different curve fit.

keys.lpn_notes_1_def: Solves one set of demands at a time, using the same gradient method EPANET uses. It does not model how the network changes over time.
keys.lpn_notes_2_def: Tanks, water quality, and control valves that open and close on their own (PRV, PSV, FCV) are not modeled. A pipe can carry a fixed minor loss, but not a valve whose open or closed state depends on the flow being solved for.
keys.lpn_notes_3_def: Every project is a tab, and every tab is saved in this browser as you work. Clearing your browser data deletes them all, so keep your work in a file: File, Save as. An asterisk on a tab means it holds changes that are not in a file. Nothing is ever written to a file unless you ask. In some browsers a project connects to the file you save it to, and File, Save writes back to that same file from then on; in others no connection is possible, so Save is disabled and only Save as is available. When a project file is kept on a shared drive, this page tells you if a colleague already has it open, so that two people do not write over each other. Because this is an early preview, please use it for small networks and for testing only.
keys.lpn_notes_5_def: A pump follows H = H₀ − aQ^b, where H is the head the pump adds and Q is the flow through it. Enter one, two, or three points from the manufacturer's curve. Three points — the head at zero flow, the normal working point, and the point of highest flow — fit H₀, a and b directly, and follow a published curve most closely. Two points fit a parabola (b = 2) with its peak at zero flow. One point uses a common rule: the head at zero flow is 1.33 × the head you enter, and the highest flow is 2 × the flow you enter, which again gives b = 2. A pump with no points entered adds no head at all. The curve is not stopped at zero, so asking a pump for more flow than its curve can deliver gives a negative head. The fix is a bigger pump or a smaller demand, not a different curve fit.
keys.lpn_notes_4_def: Scenarios, so that one project can hold several sets of demands. Tables of node and pipe results. Opening a file you used recently without hunting for it again. Reading and writing EPANET .inp files. Other languages: this page is in English only for now. Comments and suggestions are always welcome (see the feedback link above).
keys.lpn_notes_epanet_def: In August 2026 the Hazen-Williams coefficient and exponent were changed to match EPANET. Head loss results differ from earlier versions of this page by up to 0.1 percent, which is far smaller than the uncertainty in the C value itself.
